question: Is there a sphoṭa — a unitary word-entity distinct from the letters — that conveys meaning?

sides.position: Yes. The letters, perishing one after another, can convey meaning neither singly nor together; the word is a partless, sequence-less sphoṭa manifested by the sounds, grasped when the last sound, helped by the impressions of the earlier ones, makes it clear; finally only the sentence-sphoṭa is real.
arguments: a single letter would convey the whole meaning if it sufficed
we cognize 'one word', not a series
sound is a quality (dhvani) of the word, as the drum-beat's extent varies while the word stays the same

sides.position: No. 'The letters alone are the word' (Upavarṣa): the last letter, together with the impressions left by the earlier ones, conveys the meaning; a sphoṭa is never perceived and is a needless assumption.
arguments: the word is what is grasped by the ear, i.e. the letters
the impressions of earlier letters suffice

sides.position: Śaṅkara follows Upavarṣa against the sphoṭa, while accepting that the world is preceded by the Vedic word (words as eternal universals).
No separate sphoṭa: the letters are apprehended in sequence and their meaning is understood from the final letter with the recollection of the earlier ones; sound is a non-eternal quality of ether.
sides.note: Jayanta Bhaṭṭa's critique recorded from memory at work level.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: whether a unitary meaning-bearer exists over and above the letters.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the grammarians describe the word as understood (one), the Mīmāṃsakas the word as heard (letters); both agree that meaning is grasped only at the end of the utterance with the help of impressions.
P1-level: Bhartṛhari's sphoṭa belongs to the level of the undivided Word-principle, the letters to the level of articulated speech (vaikharī).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Kumārila and Śaṅkara reject any separate entity; the grammarians reject a merely serial conveyance by letters.

historical_debates.name: Maṇḍana Miśra's Sphoṭasiddhi against Kumārila
historical_debates.accounts: written reply to the Ślokavārttika's sphoṭavāda

historical_debates.name: Nāgeśa's Sphoṭavāda and the Navya-Nyāya
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: the grammarians consider the sphoṭa established

question: Is Speech at the level of paśyantī (the grammarians' Word-Brahman) the ultimate reality?

sides.position: Yes: Brahman is the beginningless Word-principle; paśyantī, undivided and with all sequence withdrawn, the inner self-light, is the supreme station of speech; all cognition is word-natured.
arguments: all cognition is interpenetrated by the word (VP 1.123)
without the word-nature of awareness there would be no illumination (VP 1.124)

sides.position: No: paśyantī is only the power of knowledge at the level of Sadāśiva; the ultimate is Śiva with will, knowledge and action, and supreme speech (parā vāk) is reflexive awareness itself, beyond paśyantī.
arguments: paśyantī still contains the seed of sequence and object
a Word-absolute without agency cannot account for the world

sides.position: The mantra manuals, accepting the four levels, place parā above paśyantī and define śabda-brahman as the consciousness of all beings rather than as word or meaning.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: which level of speech is ultimate.
candidate_readings: P1-level: all accept paśyantī as a real level; the question narrows to whether a level above it (parā) is admitted — later grammarians (Nāgeśa) themselves admit parā.

P2-standpoint: Bhartṛhari's word-nature of awareness (pratyavamarśa) and Utpaladeva's reflexive awareness (vimarśa) may name one reflexivity of consciousness from the grammarian's and the Śaiva's standpoints.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Somānanda explicitly denies that paśyantī is ultimate; the grammarians do not accept a Lord beyond the Word.

historical_debates.name: Somānanda's refutation of the grammarians (Śivadṛṣṭi ch. 2)
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: the Pratyabhijñā considers paśyantī-brahman refuted; the grammarians continue their view

question: Is the ultimate of the nature of speech (śabdādvaita), and is all cognition word-permeated?

sides.position: Yes: Brahman is the Word-principle appearing as the world; no cognition is free of the word; speech is the consciousness of beings.

No: an eternal single Word-brahman cannot produce successive, various things; if the world is its transformation it is non-eternal, if its appearance it is unreal; perception is free of words and conceptual construction.
arguments: the momentariness of all that is produced

sides.position: No: Prabhācandra refutes Word-monism among the doctrines opposed to the Jain view of many real substances and conceptual and non-conceptual cognition.
sides.note: Jain side stated at work level (low confidence).

sides.position: Śabda-brahman is not the word nor the meaning, both insentient, but the consciousness of all beings — speech is consciousness, not consciousness speech.
Supreme speech is the reflexive awareness of consciousness, not the grammarians' paśyantī.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: whether reality is Word, and whether cognition is word-permeated.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the grammarians, the mantra manuals and the Pratyabhijñā may all describe the reflexive, 'speaking' side of consciousness, differing on whether it is the whole of the ultimate.
P1-level: word-permeation may hold of conceptual (vyāvahārika) cognition, which the Buddhists also treat as word-bound, while the Buddhists deny it of perception.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Buddhists deny any permanent, single ultimate; the Jains deny monism; the Śaivas deny that paśyantī is final.

question: Does a word denote the universal (jāti, ākṛti) or the individual (vyakti, dravya)?

sides.position: Vājapyāyana: the universal form; Vyāḍi: the individual substance; Patañjali accepts both; Bhartṛhari: the universal is the true part, and ultimately all words denote Being (sattā) / the Real, as all ornament-words denote gold.
The word denotes the universal (ākṛti), which is real and eternal; the individual is understood through it.
The meaning of a word is the individual, the form and the universal together.
There are no real universals: a word signifies by excluding what is other (apoha).

reconciliation.explanation: Patañjali himself treats universal and individual as two grammatical standpoints, and Nyāya combines them; the realist schools are reconciled as standpoints.
reconciliation.detail: The reconciliation covers the realist schools only; the Buddhist apoha theory denies the reality of the universal and is not reconciled.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Buddhists reject any real universal; Mīmāṃsā insists that the universal alone is primarily denoted.

question: How does a sentence convey its meaning?

sides.position: The sentence is a single partless sphoṭa; its meaning flashes as pratibhā; word-meanings are abstractions (apoddhāra) from it; Bhartṛhari lists eight rival definitions of the sentence.
Words express their own meanings, which then combine through expectancy, compatibility and proximity (abhihitānvaya).
Words express their meanings only as already connected with one another (anvitābhidhāna).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: whether the sentence is built from words or words abstracted from the sentence.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the grammarian describes the understanding as it is experienced (one flash), the Mīmāṃsakas the analysis of how it is produced.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each school holds its account to be literally true of how meaning arises.

sides.position: Word, meaning and their relation are eternal (Kātyāyana's first vārttika); the eternal word is the sphoṭa, while the audible sounds that manifest it arise and perish.
The letters themselves are eternal and only manifested by utterance.
Sound is a non-eternal quality of ether: it has a beginning and is spoken of as produced.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled (U31 contribution adding the grammarians' distinction of sphoṭa and dhvani).
candidate_readings: P1-level: what is eternal (the word as meaning-bearer) and what is produced (the audible sound) are distinguished by the grammarians; Nyāya speaks of the audible sound only.

question: How does rasa arise from the union of determinants, consequents and transient states, and where is it?

sides.position: Lollaṭa: rasa is the stable emotion intensified by the determinants, existing in the character (Rāma) and, by imitation, in the actor.
Śaṅkuka: rasa is the stable emotion inferred in the actor, who is taken as Rāma like a painted horse taken as a horse.
Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka: rasa is neither perceived, produced nor suggested; by the powers of bhāvakatva and bhojakatva it is enjoyed in a sattva-filled repose akin to tasting Brahman.

Abhinavagupta: rasa is manifested (suggested) and relished in the sensitive spectator whose latent stable emotion is awakened by generalized determinants; it consists in the relish itself (Mammaṭa and Viśvanātha follow).

reconciliation.explanation: Abhinavagupta himself presents the earlier views as rungs of a ladder of discrimination by which the intellect climbs to the truth — a reconciliation by stages of understanding, from the tradition's own mouth.
reconciliation.detail: The reconciliation is Abhinava's; it ranks rather than equates the views. Mahimabhaṭṭa (inference) and Dhanika (purport) remain outside it.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Lollaṭa's and Śaṅkuka's own works are lost; later critics (Mahimabhaṭṭa) reject Abhinava's view of suggestion.

question: Is śānta (peace) a rasa, and what is its stable emotion?

sides.position: Yes: the Nāṭyaśāstra's śānta passage (in some recensions) makes calm its stable emotion and liberation its aim; Ānandavardhana makes it the principal rasa of the Mahābhārata; Abhinavagupta makes knowledge of reality — the self — its stable basis and the ground of all rasas; Mammaṭa (dispassion) and Viśvanātha (calm) count it the ninth.
arguments: the Mahābhārata's purport is dispassion and liberation
knowledge of reality underlies all emotions as their natural state

sides.position: No, not in drama: Bharata counts eight rasas; calm, being the cessation of all activity, cannot be developed or shown on stage (Dhanañjaya and Dhanika).
arguments: the Nāṭyaśāstra's own count is eight (NŚ 6.15)
calm cannot be represented by action

sides.position: Rūpa Gosvāmī counts śānta as the first and least intimate of the five primary devotional rasas — awareness of the Lord's greatness without personal love.

reconciliation.explanation: Much of the disagreement concerns the medium: the deniers speak of dramatic performance (nāṭya), the affirmers of poetry and of the audience's experience; in poetry both sides grant śānta.
reconciliation.detail: Abhinavagupta rejects the restriction and argues for śānta in drama too; the reconciliation holds only for the poetry/drama distinction.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Abhinavagupta insists śānta is a rasa in drama; Dhanika denies calm can be a stable emotion at all.

question: Is suggestion (dhvani, vyañjanā) a distinct power of words, and is it the soul of poetry?

sides.position: Yes: beyond denotation and indication there is an implied meaning — fact, figure or rasa — conveyed by suggestion, which is the soul of poetry (Ānandavardhana, Abhinavagupta, Mammaṭa).

No: what is called suggestion is inference from the expressed meaning; words have one power, denotation (Mahimabhaṭṭa); or rasa is conveyed by the purport of the sentence (Dhanika); or it is included in striking expression (Kuntaka).
Nāgeśa accepts suggestion (vyañjanā) as a third power of words beside denotation and indication.

reconciliation.explanation: Both sides grant that poems convey implied meanings and rasa; they differ on the cognitive operation (suggestion or inference/purport) — an analytic standpoint difference about one experience.
reconciliation.detail: The reconciliation does not decide whether the operation is inference; Ānandavardhana argues that suggestion cannot be inference because the suggested sense is not invariably concomitant.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Mahimabhaṭṭa insists that suggestion is nothing but inference; the dhvani school insists it is irreducible.

question: Is there one rasa underlying all, and if so which?

sides.position: Bharata: eight (or nine) distinct rasas, four of which generate the other four.
Bhavabhūti: compassion (karuṇa) alone is rasa, appearing as the others as water appears as eddies, bubbles and waves.
Bhoja: the one rasa is śṛṅgāra understood as self-regard (abhimāna, ahaṃkāra).
Nārāyaṇa (cited by Viśvanātha): wonder is the essence of all rasa, so the marvellous alone is rasa.
Abhinavagupta: śānta is the natural state from which all emotions arise and into which they dissolve.
Rūpa Gosvāmī: love for Kṛṣṇa (bhakti-rasa), culminating in the erotic-devotional (madhura), is the supreme rasa.

reconciliation.explanation: Each 'one rasa' names the ground of aesthetic experience from a different standpoint — pathos, self-regard, wonder, peace, love of God — while Bharata's list describes the variety as it appears.
reconciliation.detail: The theorists themselves argue for exclusive claims; the reconciliation treats their claims as complementary perspectives, which they would not all accept.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Bhoja holds that only śṛṅgāra is truly rasa; Rūpa's school holds bhakti-rasa to be rasa in the highest sense, not one perspective among others.

question: Is every rasa blissful, even compassion and terror?

sides.position: Yes: in compassion and the other rasas supreme happiness arises; the experience of the sensitive is the proof — otherwise no one would turn to the Rāmāyaṇa (Viśvanātha, following Abhinavagupta).

No: rasa is of the nature of both pleasure and pain; the compassionate, furious, odious and terrible are painful, though spectators delight in the poet's and actors' skill (Rāmacandra and Guṇacandra).

reconciliation.explanation: The Nāṭyadarpaṇa grants delight in the artistry while calling the content painful; the other side speaks of the relish as a whole — two standpoints on one experience (content vs relish).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Nāṭyadarpaṇa's authors insist the painful rasas are painful in themselves; Viśvanātha insists all rasa is bliss.

question: Can devotion to God be a full aesthetic rasa, or only a bhāva?

sides.position: Classical poetics: love directed to a deity, sage, guru or king is a bhāva, not a rasa; the rasas are eight or nine (Mammaṭa).
Rūpa Gosvāmī: love for Kṛṣṇa is the stable emotion of a true rasa, indeed the supreme one, in five primary and seven secondary forms.

reconciliation.explanation: The poeticians speak of worldly spectators' relish of poetry, Rūpa of the devotee's relish of a transcendent object — different standpoints on 'rasa'.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Rūpa's school holds bhakti-rasa to be rasa in the full and highest sense; the poeticians do not grant it rasa status.

notes: U31 contribution adding the anchored alaṅkāra side (KP 4); U16 owns the Gauḍīya side.
